title: The Battle for TV Has Shifted to the Home Screen
summary: The TV operating system has evolved beyond a simple navigation tool into a decision layer that shapes what audiences discover and ultimately watch. The companies that determine what viewers see first now have greater sway over engagement, advertising and content success.
body_markdown:
September 15, 2026


Xperi


[Geir Skaaden](https://xperi.com/news-author/geir-skaaden/)


Chief Products and Services Officer


For years, the streaming wars were largely a battle over content. The conversation centered on which services had the strongest libraries and which companies could attract audiences with the most compelling programming.


Today, that competition is entering a new era, with the battle increasingly taking place before viewers ever press play.


The TV operating system has evolved beyond a simple navigation tool into a decision layer that shapes what audiences discover and ultimately watch. The companies that determine what viewers see first now have greater sway over engagement, advertising and content success.


FOX’s announced acquisition of Roku reinforces this broader industry shift, bringing content, the operating system, discovery experience, audience relationships and monetization capabilities closer together. It underscores a fundamental change in where value is being created: not only through owning content, but through shaping the experience that leads viewers to it.


**The home screen has become the most valuable real estate in TV**


Consumers spend far less time browsing than many might assume. Viewers rarely move beyond what appears on the first screen, making prominent placement increasingly important to what ultimately gets watched.


In fact, engagement can drop 80 to 90% once content moves below the first few rows (TiVo, July 2026). That dynamic has made the TV home screen prime real estate in the streaming ecosystem.


As major streaming services compete for visibility, operating systems are becoming powerful merchandising platforms rather than simple gateways to apps. The first screen can influence which services they enter, which titles they consider and where their attention goes next.


For content providers, that changes the equation. Producing compelling programming remains essential, but earning visibility on the home screen is becoming just as critical to driving viewership, deepening engagement and strengthening retention.


**Discovery is becoming the industry’s competitive advantage**


Great content alone is no longer enough if viewers never discover it. As streaming options continue to grow, the challenge is not simply creating more programming. It is making an increasingly fragmented universe of content easier to navigate so viewers can quickly find something worth watching.


That makes discovery one of the most important factors influencing engagement. Platforms that reduce the friction between turning on the TV and finding compelling content can play an increasingly powerful role in shaping viewing behavior.


The industry is already moving in this direction. Amazon’s investment in a redesigned Fire TV experience, including enhanced recommendations and aggregated cross-service browsing, reflects a greater focus on helping consumers discover content across sources rather than steering them toward any one service. Increasingly, control belongs to whoever owns that first decision and can most effectively connect viewers with something they want to watch, not simply whoever owns the content itself.


**The home screen is reshaping advertising and personalization**


That influence extends beyond discovery. As it becomes the primary point of engagement with the connected TV experience, it is also emerging as increasingly valuable advertising inventory.


For advertisers, that creates an opportunity to engage viewers before they have decided what to watch. What was once viewed primarily as a navigation experience is becoming an important part of the monetization opportunity around connected TV.


At the same time, consumer expectations are evolving. Viewers increasingly expect the first screen to do more than present apps or basic recommendations. Personalized recommendations, previews and richer discovery experiences can help audiences make decisions more easily and move quickly from browsing to watching.


Personalization, therefore, is shifting from simply recommending a show toward creating a more intuitive viewing experience. The goal is not personalization for its own sake, but to reduce friction and help viewers find relevant content faster.


**The next chapter belongs to the decision layer**


The home screen will continue to evolve as the center of the connected TV experience.


AI and increasingly intelligent personalization will accelerate that shift, allowing platforms to better understand viewer intent and adapt discovery experiences in real time. In turn, the operating system will become an increasingly important foundation connecting discovery, advertising and consumer engagement.


The next generation of the TV home screen will move beyond static app rows and banner advertisements. Instead, it will become a living, AI-powered experience layer that connects viewers with relevant content regardless of source, while creating new opportunities for engagement and monetization.


The streaming wars may have started with a race to build the strongest content libraries, but the next chapter will be defined by who can make the broader universe of available programming the easiest to navigate. As the industry moves forward, the platforms that succeed will make a fragmented content landscape feel simple, relevant and intuitive for viewers.
